narrative:
The model estimates a 28% probability that you will fail your final year. That is not a certainty, but it is a meaningful risk: roughly one in four students with a similar profile would not pass. Because the school treats that level of risk as high enough to require action, you are being directed to remedial courses.

The prediction was driven most strongly by your record of no past class failures. This was the top factor and it worked in your favour, pushing the estimate toward passing. The second most influential factor was your father’s education level. It is primary-level, which is less common among students who passed: only about 13.8% of passers had a father at that level, compared with larger shares at 5–9th grade, secondary, or higher. This factor pushed toward failing. The third factor was your reason for choosing this school: because it is close to home. This played a smaller role and pushed slightly toward passing.

To improve your position, focus on what you can change. Your weekly study time is under two hours, while most students who passed studied two to five hours or more, so building a consistent study routine is the clearest next step. You also have no school support and no paid lessons, so ask teachers for structured help and use any available internet or library access. Keep attending regularly and seek support early rather than waiting until exams.
